audience.notes: Australian couples in their 30s, AUD 150K+, planning a luxury or destination wedding. Witty, articulate, nervous about sounding cringe in front of parents, grandparents and overseas guests. Paying parents care that the ceremony stays dignified.

payload.search_intent: Informational: inspiration plus a how-to for writing vows that are funny without losing sincerity.
payload.angle: A writing guide, not a joke list. Funny vows land when each laugh sets up a real promise. Anchor it in what Australian law still requires (Marriage Act 1961 s 45 words and the celebrant's monitum), give a simple repeatable structure, offer our own original lines clearly labelled as illustrations, and show how humour changes at a destination or symbolic ceremony abroad, which is where a Wedded Advisor and your celebrant quietly handle the legal ceremony, sound, timing and translation.
serp_gaps_to_win: Legal anchor: no ranking page mentions the s 45 words or the monitum, or that personal vows sit alongside them.
Structure: lists everywhere, almost no method for balancing jokes with a real promise.
Destination delivery: humour across languages and cultures, outdoor sound, officiants abroad, symbolic versus legal ceremonies.
Kind humour: guidance on avoiding jokes at a partner's or family's expense, which many lists ignore.
Fresh, original lines (competitors recycle the same fries, keys and snoring jokes).

outline.h2: What makes a funny vow still mean something
outline.answers: Can vows be funny without being flippant?
must_include: Laugh, then land: every joke should set up a sincere promise
Humour that is specific to the two of you beats generic one-liners (answers fear: ending up with something generic)
Short intro paragraph answers the query in 2 to 3 sentences for the AI Overview and featured snippet

outline.h2: The legal words you still need in Australia
outline.answers: Can we replace the official vows with funny ones?
must_include: Marriage Act 1961 s 45(2): each party must say the prescribed words (or words to that effect) in the presence of the celebrant and witnesses; quote the wording exactly from the source and link legislation.gov.au inline at the claim

The monitum: an authorised celebrant (not a minister of religion of a recognised denomination) must say the s 46 words before the marriage; link the Attorney-General's Department (ag.gov.au) or legislation.gov.au inline
Personal funny vows go alongside the legal words, never instead of them; your celebrant can place them before or after
Descriptive link to /expert-advice/traditional-wedding-vows (never the anchor 'traditional wedding vows') and to /expert-advice/simple-wedding-ceremony-script for where the legal lines sit
Researcher must verify exact s 45 and s 46 text and current URLs; no paraphrase presented as a quote

outline.h2: A simple structure for funny vows
outline.answers: How do I actually write them?
must_include: 4-part pattern: an opener that names a shared truth, one or two light jokes, the turn, the real promise
Length: about one minute spoken, roughly 120 to 180 words each (writer to state as guidance, not a statistic)
Agree tone and length with your partner, not the words
Link /expert-advice/wedding-vows-for-her and /expert-advice/wedding-vows-for-him for more examples

outline.h2: Humour that lands and humour to avoid
outline.answers: Which jokes are safe in front of grandparents?
must_include: Self-deprecating and shared-habit humour lands; ex-partners, in-laws, bodies, money and in-jokes nobody else gets do not
Test it on one trusted friend, not the group chat
Think about the paying parents and older guests

outline.h2: Funny wedding vow examples you can adapt
outline.answers: Can you give me lines to start from?
must_include: 8 to 12 ORIGINAL lines written by us, labelled as illustrations
Each joke paired with its sincere turn
Light destination flavour (jet lag, the villa Wi-Fi, packing, the long-haul flight) without naming real venues or couples
No lines copied or adapted from competitor pages; no vows attributed to real couples or celebrities

outline.h2: Funny vows at a destination or symbolic ceremony
outline.answers: Does any of this change if we marry overseas?
must_include: Many couples marry legally in Australia and hold a symbolic ceremony abroad, where wording is free; if marrying legally overseas, that country's rules apply (no specifics unless sourced)
Link /expert-advice/weddings-abroad-where-can-you-legally-get-married and /expert-advice/overseas-marriage-certificate

Invisible work: interpreters or bilingual cards for overseas family, jokes that do not translate, wind and sound outdoors (microphone for the couple, not just the celebrant), sunset timing, a printed copy kept by the planner
Optional: link /destination-weddings/civil-ceremony-in-italy-vs-catholic-and-symbolic-rites as one example
Soft CTA: a Wedded Advisor coordinates celebrant, sound and timing so the vows are the only thing you think about

outline.h2: How to deliver funny vows on the day
outline.answers: How do I not freeze or rush the punchline?
must_include: Read from a card or a small book, not a phone
Pause after the laugh; let it finish before the turn
Rehearse aloud twice, once with the celebrant
Keep vow cards as a keepsake; link /expert-advice/humorous-wedding-ceremony-script for a whole funny ceremony
Can wedding vows be funny and still legal in Australia?
How long should funny wedding vows be?
Should we tell each other our vows before the wedding?
Can we use funny vows at a vow renewal? (link /celebration-ideas/vow-renewal-vows)
What if one of us is funny and the other is not?
